children.value: The midterm assessment for Condensed Matter I is a
written proposal for your final presentation project

The purpose of the proposal is to make sure that, well before the final examination, you have identified a meaningful condensed matter physics question and developed a concrete plan for understanding it.
“I want to give my final presentation on topological insulators.”
is a topic choice, but it is not yet a proposal.
A successful proposal should make clear:

What physical question will I investigate? Why is it nontrivial? What is the simplest model or theoretical framework that captures the physics? What calculation or argument will I use? What do I expect to learn?
The proposal represents the first stage of your final project:

children.html: topic→question→minimal model→method→expected physics\boxed{ \text{topic} \rightarrow \text{question} \rightarrow \text{minimal model} \rightarrow \text{method} \rightarrow \text{expected physics} }topic→question→minimal model→method→expected physics​

3. Relationship Between the Midterm and Final Examination

children.label: 3. Relationship Between the Midterm and Final Examination

children.value: At the midterm stage, you should establish

children.html: Question+Model+Preliminary Understanding+Plan\boxed{ \text{Question} + \text{Model} + \text{Preliminary Understanding} + \text{Plan} }Question+Model+Preliminary Understanding+Plan​

children.value: By the final examination, this should develop into

children.html: Question→Model→Derivation / Evidence→Physical Understanding\boxed{ \text{Question} \rightarrow \text{Model} \rightarrow \text{Derivation / Evidence} \rightarrow \text{Physical Understanding} }Question→Model→Derivation / Evidence→Physical Understanding​

children.value: The most important development between the two stages is therefore
not simply adding more references, calculations, or slides
It is turning your proposed question into an argument that you genuinely understand.
Present the completed project and explain its central physical result
Defend your reasoning and answer questions related to your project
Demonstrate broader understanding of Condensed Matter I
The three components test different abilities.
Your final presentation should develop the proposal into a coherent physical argument:

children.html: Question→Minimal Model→Derivation / Evidence→Result→Physical Interpretation\boxed{ \text{Question} \rightarrow \text{Minimal Model} \rightarrow \text{Derivation / Evidence} \rightarrow \text{Result} \rightarrow \text{Physical Interpretation} }Question→Minimal Model→Derivation / Evidence→Result→Physical Interpretation​

children.value: The goal is not to present everything you learned about the topic.
Instead, your presentation should answer a specific physical question.
By the end of the presentation, your audience should understand:
what calculation or argument produced the key result;
After the presentation, you will answer questions related to your project.
These questions may ask you to:
explain one of your equations physically;
reproduce or reconstruct a simple argument;
predict what happens when a parameter changes;
distinguish essential ingredients from unnecessary ones;
connect your project to another concept from the course;
reason through a situation that was not explicitly included in your presentation.

4.3 General Condensed Matter Physics Oral Examination — 15 minutes

children.label: 4.3 General Condensed Matter Physics Oral Examination — 15 minutes

children.value: The final 15 minutes will contain broader questions from Condensed Matter I.
not restricted to your final-project topic
The emphasis will be on physical reasoning and connections among the major concepts of the course.
You should expect follow-up questions such as:
What happens if I change this parameter?
What breaks if I remove this assumption?
Can you give me the simplest example?
The objective is to evaluate whether you can
, rather than only reproduce prepared material.
5. The Overall Logic of the Project

children.label: 5. The Overall Logic of the Project

children.value: The project is designed to develop in stages over the semester.
Through the homework assignments, you learn how to work with the central theoretical tools and concepts of condensed matter physics.

children.html: I know what I want to understand and how I plan to investigate it.\boxed{ \text{I know what I want to understand and how I plan to investigate it.} }I know what I want to understand and how I plan to investigate it.​

children.value: Final — Explain and Defend the Physics

children.label: Final — Explain and Defend the Physics

children.html: I now understand the physics well enough to explain it and reason with it.\boxed{ \text{I now understand the physics well enough to explain it and reason with it.} }I now understand the physics well enough to explain it and reason with it.​

children.value: The overall progression of the course is therefore:

children.html: Learn the tools→Formulate a problem→Investigate it→Explain it→Defend your understanding\boxed{ \text{Learn the tools} \rightarrow \text{Formulate a problem} \rightarrow \text{Investigate it} \rightarrow \text{Explain it} \rightarrow \text{Defend your understanding} }Learn the tools→Formulate a problem→Investigate it→Explain it→Defend your understanding​

children.value: This progression is more important than simply obtaining a correct final answer.
The final project is not intended to test how much information you can collect about a topic.
It is intended to test whether you can take a condensed matter physics problem and progressively make it your own.
At the midterm, you should be able to say:
I know what question I am asking, why it is interesting, what model I should use, and what I still need to figure out.
By the final examination, you should be able to say:
I can now explain what happens, why it happens, what assumptions are required, and how this example connects to the broader principles of condensed matter physics.
owning the physical reasoning behind the answer
—is the central goal of the project.
